unit.title: Edo and the floating world
unit.question: How did a city turn pictures into a mass market, and who got named when it did?

beats.text:
On 3 July 2024 Japan issued a new thousand-yen note. On its back is this wave, caught just before it breaks, with Mount Fuji small behind it.
The picture was printed in Edo around 1831. It sold for about the price of two bowls of noodles.
Eleven years later, the state that now prints it on money banned half of what the trade sold, and capped the price of the rest.

This unit asks one question. **How did a city turn pictures into a mass market, and who got named when it did?**
You will follow five publishers’ bets, one to an act. You will also follow one sheet of paper, from Echizen to New York.
The map and the timeline move as you read. Tap any name, place or year to open it.

segments.title: A city built to be an audience

predict.q: In 1721 Edo counted its people for the first time. About how many lived there?
predict.explain: About 1.3 million by the city’s own count, samurai and townspeople in nearly equal numbers. The buyers came before the pictures.

beats.text:
In 1603 [[ieyasu]] became shogun and made Edo, a castle town on a marshy bay, the seat of his government.
The emperor stayed in Kyoto. Osaka stayed the country’s warehouse.
From 1635 every lord in Japan had to live in Edo in alternate years, leaving his wife and heir behind when he went home.
Their processions filled the roads. Their households filled the city.

In the first month of 1657 a fire broke out at Honmyō-ji temple in Hongō, at about two in the afternoon.
The next morning a second fire started in Koishikawa. That afternoon a third began in Kōjimachi.
Between sixty and seventy per cent of the city burned, and the castle keep was never rebuilt.
The dead are counted at anything from thirty thousand to a hundred thousand.

The rebuilt city spread east. A bridge at Ryōgoku crossed the Sumida, and the districts of Honjo and Fukagawa grew on the far bank.
The fire also moved the licensed quarter. It had stood near Nihonbashi since 1617.
After 1657 it was rebuilt in the rice fields north of Asakusa, behind a moat with a single gate, as the Shin-Yoshiwara.

figure.cap: Picture book of play synopses for the Nakamura theatre, dated 1799 · Torii-school artist · The Met 2013.851 · CC0

beats.text:
Edo’s leisure ran through two licensed businesses. Three kabuki theatres stood in the town centre, at Sakai-chō, Fukiya-chō and Kobiki-chō.
The quarter stood at the edge.
Both sold glamour to a city with time and money, and both needed advertising.
Because the state licensed them, it could later ban them by name.

Pictures had been printed from woodblocks in Japan for centuries, mostly Buddhist images and book illustrations.
In the 1670s Edo began trading pictures as goods. [[moronobu]] signed his book pictures from 1672, and the earliest known single sheets follow.
The trade called its subject *ukiyo*, the floating world: once a Buddhist word for a sorrowful world, now the world of passing pleasures.

A print was never one hand. The **publisher** planned it, paid for it, applied for permission and sold it.
The **designer** drew it on thin paper. The **carver** pasted that drawing face down on cherry wood and cut through it, destroying it.
The **printer** inked the blocks and rubbed each sheet by hand.
This is a carver’s key block, pulled in black. The notches outside the picture registered every colour block that followed.

Full colour arrived in a single year, and not from the trade.
For New Year 1765, circles of amateur poets commissioned picture calendars to exchange at parties. They paid for the best designers, carvers and paper.
Publishers then bought the blocks, cut out the patrons’ names and sold the sheets as *nishiki-e*, brocade pictures (probable).
The poets’ favourite designer was [[harunobu]]. He had five years left to live.

decide.q: Who paid for the first full-colour prints in 1765?
options: Circles of amateur poets, for gifts
decide.explain: Poetry circles commissioned them as New Year calendars. The trade sold them afterwards.

predict.q: From 1790, whom did the law hold responsible for a print?
options: The designer, the writer and the publisher
Everyone who worked on it, carver and printer included
predict.explain: The designer, the writer and the publisher. The carver and the printer were never named in the law.

beats.text:
[[tsutaya]] was born in the Shin-Yoshiwara in 1750 and grew up there.
His first business was a bookshop on the road to the quarter’s gate. His first product was its printed guide, the *Yoshiwara saiken*, which he came to publish alone.
In 1783 he moved into the city, to Tōri Abura-chō by Nihonbashi, the street of the big houses.
His seal was an ivy leaf under a three-peaked Fuji.

This is what a print shop looked like, drawn by Hokusai for a picture book of 1802. The Tokyo Metropolitan Library identifies it as Tsutaya’s own shop (probable).
Sheets hang in the front, books lie in piles.
Publishers sold from their shops, swapped stock with each other and supplied street sellers.
Some 655 lending libraries carried books door to door in 1808.

figure.cap: Utagawa Hiroshige, Cherry Blossom Time in Nakanochō, the quarter’s main street · LACMA via Wikimedia Commons · public domain

beats.text:
The quarter’s women were there under contract. A typical indenture around 1800, signed by a father, exchanged a lump sum for years of service: for instance 25 ryō for five.
Debts for food, clothes and medicine could extend the term.
From 1793 the only women prints could name were courtesans. [[hanaogi]] wrote poetry admired in her day. In 1794 she ran away, and was brought back.

In 1787 [[sadanobu]] became chief councillor and began the Kansei reforms, against a decade of famine and spending.
From the fifth month of 1790 publishers had to submit every design to censors chosen from their own guild.
Approval was a small round seal reading *kiwame*, “examined”, cut into the key block.
On this Utamaro, Tsutaya’s ivy leaf and the censor’s seal sit side by side.

The seal came with examples. In 1791 three of Kyōden’s comic books, published by Tsutaya, were judged offensive.
[[kyoden]] was manacled for fifty days. Tsutaya was fined half of everything he owned.
More rules followed: no women named on prints except courtesans, and from 1800 no large bust portraits of women.
The stated reason was that they were “conspicuous”.

Tsutaya answered the fine with luxury. [[utamaro]]’s bust portraits of women on powdered mica were the luxury prints of the decade.
Then, in the fifth month of 1794, he issued actor portraits by an unknown designer signed [[sharaku]].
About 140 designs followed in ten months, all for Tsutaya. Then nothing.
Nobody knows who Sharaku was.

Osaka ran the same medium another way.
In the eighth month of 1793 the publisher [[shioya]] won the sole right to publish actor likenesses. In 1794 he bought a rival artist’s blocks.
That artist, [[ryukosai]], “never put his signature” on the prints Shioya made from his designs, and withdrew.
In Osaka, fan clubs and poetry circles paid for much of the trade.

Tsutaya died in 1797, aged 47. His shop went on under his name.
In 1804 Utamaro was manacled for fifty days for a print of the warlord Hideyoshi, a subject the state treated as its own. He died two years later.
The golden age ended in handcuffs twice.
The censor now held the publisher answerable for every sheet. What would a publisher dare to bet on next?

decide.q: On the Utamaro sheet, which mark is the state’s?
options: The small round seal reading kiwame
decide.explain: The kiwame seal. Every legal sheet carried it from 1790 until 1842; the band on the timeline is its reign.

segments.title: The old man and the pigment

predict.q: Where was the blue in a Great Wave sold in 1831 made?
options: Abroad: in Europe and, by then, mostly in China
predict.explain: Never in Japan in this period. It came by ship to Nagasaki, and from 1824 Chinese supply made it cheap.

beats.text:
Act II begins inside the wave. Look at the hollow under the claw, where three boats lie low in the water.
That blue was new in 1831. It is the reason this sheet exists.

[[hokusai]] was born in Edo in 1760. Between 16 and 19 he trained to cut woodblocks.
He then studied under the actor-print designer [[shunsho]], signing himself Shunrō, and Tsutaya published some of his early work.
In 1807 Edo’s picture publishers formed a guild, the *jihon toiya*, which owned the blocks and policed copying.
Hokusai would be over seventy before his most famous sheet.

In 1814 a Nagoya publisher, [[eirakuya]], began issuing the *Hokusai Manga*. These were sketchbooks of people, animals, gods and things, sold as models for amateurs.
This copy of the first volume is a later printing, after 1828.
The books made Hokusai a brand outside Edo. Whether they make him the “father of manga” is still a question, even in a British Museum curator’s title.

Prussian blue was first made in Berlin around 1704, by accident: a colour-maker’s red came out blue.
It reached Japan the only way European goods could, by ship to Nagasaki, where Edo called it *bero-ai*, “Berlin indigo”.
Dutch ships brought it via the Cape and Batavia.
Then, from 1824, Chinese junks re-entered the trade “in steadily increasing quantities”.

argued.q: When did Prussian blue reach Edo’s printers?

a.title: Around 1790
a.text: One reading has it arriving through Dejima around 1790 and staying costly until about 1820.

b.title: In the late 1820s
b.text: Another has it known but little used until Chinese imports from 1824 made it cheap enough for a sixteen-mon sheet.

argued.evidence: Between 1824 and 1828 the Nagasaki price fell “from 87 to 31 monme” a kin, and the Dutch withdrew from the trade.
argued.why: The price fall is what turned a luxury into a print colour. It supports the later date for printers, without denying earlier arrivals.

beats.text:
Historians agree the blue came by sea. They disagree about when Edo’s printers could afford it.
The line on the timeline is Henry Smith’s figure for the Chinese price at Nagasaki, from 87 to 31 monme of silver a kin.
Read both positions, then decide which the price supports.

In 1829 the fan-maker [[iseya]] put out a fan by [[eisen]] printed in light and dark shades of the new blue alone.
By the bookseller [[toho]]’s account it was a sensation, and other fan-makers flooded the market with all-blue fans.
This Eisen sheet, from the early 1830s, is printed the same way: one imported colour, in gradations, on white paper.

Then, Tōho says, [[nishimuraya]] of Bakuro-chō issued Hokusai’s *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji* in the new blue. It was “a great fad, double that of the fans.”
His advertisement, printed for New Year 1831, promised one view to a sheet and “more than one hundred, without being limited to thirty-six”.
Thirty-six became forty-six. This is Red Fuji, one of the first.

decide.q: By Tōho’s account, who started the blue fad?
options: A fan-maker, with an Eisen fan
The Dutch, with a gift to the shogun
decide.explain: Iseya Sōbei’s Eisen fan of 1829. Eijudō followed with Hokusai’s Fuji series.

predict.q: Is the Great Wave a tsunami?
options: No: a storm wave about ten metres high
predict.explain: Scientists who studied it read a plunging storm wave, about ten metres high and three kilometres offshore. Tsunamis travel low out at sea.

beats.text:
The title places the scene “off Kanagawa”, a post station on the bay road south of Edo. Fuji stands about eighty kilometres west.
Three long boats ride a swell, their crews bent at the oars.
Two scientists who studied the picture concluded Hokusai drew “an exceptionally large storm wave”. Another team put it near ten metres, about three kilometres offshore.

The Met examined its Great Waves with a spectrometer.
The dark stripes of the wave mix the new Prussian blue with old indigo.
The deep hollow is pure Prussian blue, printed twice.
Those are decisions about blocks and ink, made in a workshop. The sheet credits one man: 北斎改為一筆, “Hokusai, changing his name to Iitsu, drew this.”

Here the Met’s image is separated by colour, one layer per ink. Drag the slider to lay them down.
A real edition needed a block for each colour, cut by hand and registered to the notches.
One printer could pull about two hundred sheets a day. A publisher needed to sell about two thousand to profit.

There is no single Great Wave. There is an edition, pulled from the same blocks over months or years as the wood wore down.
By 2020 the British Museum had located 111 impressions, ordered in eight states; by 2024, 113.
No block survives. The most quoted estimate, up to 8,000 sheets, is an inference from wear (argued).
Compare three originals.

a.title: Hokusai
a.text: The design is one man’s, made at seventy after fifty years of drawing. In 1834 he wrote that by 110 every dot and line would live (probable).

b.title: A system
b.text: A publisher’s bet, a pigment’s price, a carver who cut the foam and a printer who pulled the blue twice. Only one is named.

argued.evidence: The hollow was printed twice in pure Prussian blue.
argued.why: Mostly B: double printing was the printer’s work, even if the designer asked for it. The sheet shows a team; the signature shows one name.

beats.text:
Two readings of authorship meet in this sheet. One is the genius in the signature. The other is the trade that made it.
Hokusai’s own workshop complicates both: his daughter [[oi]] painted inside it.
Weigh the evidence, then choose.

This night scene in the Yoshiwara is by Katsushika Ōi. Only about ten works are confirmed as hers.
Hokusai “is reported to have said” her pictures of women were better than his.
Orders sent to “Hokusai” could be painted by father or daughter and signed with his name (probable).
One historian argues her hand was made to vanish, “for profit”.

Hokusai knew whose hands mattered.
In 1835 he wanted a particular carver, [[egawa]], for his *One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji*. To get him, he offered to give up his own share of the carving fee.
The letter implies designers normally took a cut of the carver’s pay for bringing the work.
It is one of very few records of what a carver was worth.

In 1833–34 [[hiroshige]] designed the *Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō* for the publisher [[hoeido]]: fifty-five sheets from Nihonbashi to Kyoto.
The Tōkaidō was the lords’ road between the two capitals.
Some sheets were reprinted twelve to fifteen thousand times, by the usual estimate.
Watch the road draw itself, station by station.

decide.q: Put these in order: the Tōkaidō series, the Thirty-six Views, the ban on actor prints.
decide.explain: Fuji in 1831, the road in 1833, the ban in 1842. The landscapes came first.

acts.title: The ban and the hundred views

predict.q: In 1842 the state capped the price of a print. By about how much did it cut an ordinary ten-colour sheet?
predict.explain: About a third: from about 24 mon to 16, the price of one bowl of soba.

beats.text:
A record of 1805 prices an ordinary sheet at twenty mon. A bowl of *kake-soba* cost sixteen.
A picture cost about a meal, which is what made it a mass product.
In 1841 [[tadakuni]] began the Tenpō reforms, a second attempt to discipline the city’s spending.
The price lane on the timeline is about to change.

In the sixth month of 1842 the town order reached the prints.
「錦絵と唱、歌舞伎役者遊女女芸者等を壱枚摺ニ致候義、風俗ニ拘り候筋ニ付」
Single sheets of kabuki actors, courtesans and geisha “concern public morals”. Their publication, and the sale of existing stock, were forbidden.
Subjects should be loyalty, filial piety, chastity and children’s moral instruction.

In the eleventh month came the price.
「壱枚絵団扇絵共、拾六文以上は無用之事」: single sheets and fan prints, nothing above sixteen mon.
Printings were limited to seven or eight, and sets to three sheets (probable).
An ordinary ten-colour sheet had sold for about twenty-four. The state had banned the trade’s two best sellers and cut the price of the rest by a third.

figure.cap: Utagawa Kunisada, the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, 1826 · Art Institute of Chicago 1937.270 · CC0

beats.text:
The three theatres were ordered out of the city centre to a new street, Saruwaka-chō, near the road to the Yoshiwara.
The state put its licensed pleasures together, at the edge.
[[danjuro]], the most famous actor in Japan, was banished from Edo for extravagance (probable).
Watch the theatres move.

The censor’s machine changed with the subjects.
From 1843 ward headmen, *nanushi*, stamped prints with their own names: one seal, then two from 1847, then two with a date.
From 1853 a single seal reading *aratame*, “examined”, usually came with a date seal.
So a sheet’s margin dates it to within a few years. Remember the four bands.

The ban made warriors the safest genre, and [[kuniyoshi]] had drawn them since 1827.
In 1847 he gave the trade the loyal retainers of the forty-seven rōnin, one to a sheet, fifty-one in all. The censor [[murata]] approved them.
The [[fujiokaya]] records 8,000 sets sold between the seventh month of 1847 and the third of 1848.
The same diary records a flop.

argued.q: Did the ban create the landscape print?

a.title: Yes
a.text: With actors and beauties forbidden, views of famous places became the safe product, and the trade poured into them.

b.title: No: it sped it up
b.text: The Fuji series was out in 1831 and the Tōkaidō in 1833. The ban protected a genre already selling, and pushed the trade towards warriors.

argued.evidence: A magistrate reported in 1847 that six or seven tenths of what sold were actor pictures “without names”: warriors with actors’ faces.
argued.why: The trade routed around the ban with disguised actors, not mainly with landscapes, which were already a market.

beats.text:
A common story says the ban made the landscape print.
The dates on the timeline complicate it, and so does what a magistrate found when he counted the shops five years later.
Weigh the two readings.

The edict named actors, courtesans and geisha. It did not name ghosts, monsters or cats.
Kuniyoshi drew all three. This is the monster cat of Okazaki, from a ghost play set on the Tōkaidō: a cat, a play and an actor’s face at once.
The ban sharpened the trade’s talent for saying one thing with another.

decide.q: At about 200 impressions a day, how many working days does one printer need for 8,000 impressions of one sheet?
decide.explain: Forty days for one sheet. The loyal-retainers series had fifty-one, so it needed many printers working at once.

segments.title: A hundred views of a city about to be renamed

predict.q: Commodore Perry sailed from Virginia to Japan in 1852–53. Which way did he go?
options: East, across the Atlantic and Indian Oceans
predict.explain: East: Madeira, the Cape, Mauritius, Ceylon, Singapore and China, eight months to Uraga.

beats.text:
[[perry]] left Hampton Roads, Virginia, on 24 November 1852.
He crossed the Atlantic to Madeira, rounded the Cape of Good Hope, called at Mauritius, Ceylon and Singapore, and gathered his ships in China.
On 8 July 1853 four American ships anchored off Uraga, at the mouth of Edo Bay.
A treaty followed in 1854.

On 11 November 1855 an earthquake struck Edo, and thousands died.
Within two days the shops were selling *namazu-e*, pictures of the giant catfish said to cause earthquakes. One study counts about 380 kinds (probable).
Most were unsigned and uncensored. Here the god of Kashima pins the catfish with his sword.
The trade moved at the speed of news.

Between 1856 and 1858 Hiroshige designed the *One Hundred Famous Views of Edo* for the publisher [[uoya]]. There are 118 views, with a title page by another hand.
Every view stood somewhere you could walk to. Each dot on this map of 1859 is one of them, coloured by season.
Tap any dot to see the sheet. Hiroshige died in 1858, as the set was being finished.

This is one of the hundred views: a sudden shower over the Shin-Ōhashi bridge, 1857.
Everything the sheet says about its own making sits outside the picture.
Tap each mark. Then date the sheet from its seals alone, the way a curator does first.

figure.cap: Utagawa Yoshikazu, Americans Baking Bread, 1861 · Art Institute of Chicago 1926.1692 · CC0

beats.text:
In 1859 a fishing village on the Kanagawa shore, close to where Hokusai set his wave, became the treaty port of Yokohama.
Foreign merchants, ships and households arrived.
Within a year or two Edo’s publishers were selling *Yokohama-e*, prints of the newcomers at work and at home.
It was the last new genre the Edo trade invented.

In 1864 synthetic aniline dyes arrived, and the palette of the last prints turned to hard reds and purples.
In 1868 the shogunate fell, the emperor moved to Edo, and the city was renamed Tokyo.
In 1872 a decree cancelled the debts of the Yoshiwara’s women (probable).
The trade did not end. It was about to find its best customers.

decide.q: Which seal tells you a sheet was printed after 1853?
decide.explain: Aratame, “examined”, with a date seal: the system from 1853 until about 1875.

acts.title: The second trade
acts.kicker: Act IV · 1865–1928 · Hayashi, Bing and Wright

predict.q: Did ukiyo-e reach Europe as wrapping paper for porcelain?
options: A legend: the first printed account describes a bound book used to wedge porcelain
predict.explain: The earliest printed source, from 1905, describes a small bound book used to wedge porcelain in a crate. Nothing shows sheets used as wrapping.

beats.text:
In 1865 French mail steamers opened a branch line to Yokohama.
In 1867 Japan showed at the Paris exposition, the shogunate’s last year.
After the Suez Canal opened in 1869, the Messageries Maritimes ran through-sailings from Marseille to Yokohama, from April 1870.
Prints, books, lacquer and porcelain now had a regular road to Europe.

A famous story says Europe found ukiyo-e as packing paper.
Its earliest printed source is a memoir of 1905. At the printer Delâtre’s, the engraver Bracquemond found “un petit livre bizarrement broché”, a small oddly bound book, wedging porcelain.
It was a volume of the Manga, not loose sheets, and its date of 1856 is disputed.
Retellings turned it into wrapping paper.

[[hayashi]] came to Paris as an interpreter for the exposition of 1878 and opened a shop in 1884.
Over eleven years he made 218 shipments from Japan.
One count gives 166,000 prints and 9,708 illustrated books. Another says more than 300,000 works (argued).
The second trade had a Japanese dealer at its centre.

[[bing]], a Hamburg-born dealer in Paris, published *Le Japon artistique* from 1888 to 1891: thirty-six issues in French, English and German.
In 1890 he hung over seven hundred prints at the École des Beaux-Arts.
His shop would later give a name to Art Nouveau.
The painters came to look.

[[vangogh]] bought about 660 Japanese prints in early 1887 and hung some in a Paris café.
That autumn he painted three copies in oil. Two were after Hiroshige: a plum orchard, and the sudden shower over Shin-Ōhashi. The third copied a courtesan by Eisen.
The copies are in Amsterdam. The museum’s licence is non-commercial, so they are linked, not shown.

a.title: Exchange
a.text: Japan showed itself at Paris on purpose, Japanese dealers chose and sold the prints, and European art changed for good.

b.title: Appropriation
b.text: Europe took the forms without the makers, prized single sheets as curios, and named the borrowing after itself: Japonisme.

argued.evidence: A Japanese dealer, Hayashi, chose and shipped much of what Paris saw.
argued.why: Mostly A for this evidence: the selection was Japanese. The B reading still holds for how the prints were displayed and credited.

beats.text:
The borrowing has a name, *Japonisme*, and a counter-name, appropriation.
Both describe something real.
Weigh one piece of evidence against the two readings.

predict.q: Who curated Japan’s first exhibition of ukiyo-e, in Tokyo in 1898?
predict.explain: Fenollosa, Boston’s curator of Japanese art. Japan’s own first show of its popular prints was organised by an American.

beats.text:
From 1 January 1867 Pacific Mail steamers ran from San Francisco to Yokohama. From 1869 a railroad crossed America.
Boston bought first and most.
[[fenollosa]] became the Museum of Fine Arts’ first curator of Japanese art. In 1898 he curated Japan’s first exhibition of ukiyo-e, in Tokyo.

In 1921 the brothers William and John Spaulding gave Boston’s Museum of Fine Arts more than six thousand prints. Their one condition was that the prints never be exhibited.
They may be studied, and never shown.
The museum now holds more than forty-five thousand Japanese prints.
The afterlife had licence rules of its own.

[[wright]] first went to Japan in 1905. In 1906 he lent the Art Institute of Chicago a whole exhibition of Hiroshige.
He dealt in prints for twenty years. A deal with the Spauldings in 1913 grew from twenty thousand dollars to 125,000 in five months.
This Plum Garden at Kameido names him in its provenance: sold to Kate Buckingham, February 1915.

In 1919–20 some prints Wright had sold proved “revamped”: faded impressions recut and recoloured, with pinholes where new blocks were registered.
The fraud was traced to a Tokyo dealer and a collector, and cost Wright about thirty thousand dollars in refunds.
In 1928 his bank seized his house. Thousands of his prints sold at a dollar each.

In 1889 [[tokuno]], head of Japan’s government Printing Bureau, sent the Smithsonian a complete printing set. It held blocks, tools, pigments and over a hundred progressive proofs.
Its records name the carver [[kido]] and the printers [[yamamoto]] and [[nakamura]].
A century of nameless carvers and printers got names only when the state sent the trade abroad.

decide.q: Which collection may never be exhibited, by its donors’ condition?
decide.explain: The Spaulding gift of 1921: more than six thousand prints, to be studied and never shown.

acts.title: The icon
acts.kicker: Act V · 2020–2024 · the Bank of Japan

predict.q: How many original impressions of the Great Wave are known today?
predict.explain: 113 located by 2024. Eight thousand is an estimate of how many were printed; twenty-one was an old guess.

beats.text:
Follow one sheet. Its paper was probably *hōsho* of paper-mulberry, the kind Echizen was famous for.
It was cut, inked and printed in Edo for Eijudō of Bakuro-chō, about 1831, and sold for sixteen to twenty mon.
How it crossed the Pacific is not recorded. In 1929 it entered the Met in the Havemeyer bequest, as JP1847.

The census goes on. By 2020 the British Museum had located 111 Great Waves, in eight states. Red Fuji has 93 known impressions in five.
The Met holds all forty-six Fuji designs, in 121 impressions.
None of the blocks survives, and no record of the print run exists.
Every count is a museum’s, not a publisher’s.

On 3 July 2024 the Bank of Japan put the wave on the back of the thousand-yen note.
The note’s image is not openly licensed, so it is described here, not shown.
A publisher bet this sheet on a pigment fad. A censor stamped it, and a later state capped its price. Now the state prints it as money.

Five bets. Tsutaya answered a fine with luxury. Eijudō bet on a pigment’s price. The ban turned the trade to warriors and views.
Hayashi, Bing and Wright made a second trade abroad. The Bank of Japan made an icon.
The designers were named on every sheet. The carvers and printers were named once, in 1889, for export.

Six last questions, one tap each, from across the unit.
Then the map and the timeline are yours: every place, year and name opens.

groups.title: Publishers
groups.note: They planned the title, paid for blocks, paper and labour, applied to the censor and sold the sheets. From 1790 the law held them answerable.

groups.title: Designers
groups.note: They drew the picture that the carver cut through and destroyed. Theirs is usually the only name on the sheet.

groups.title: Carvers and printers
groups.note: The two most skilled trades in the chain, and the least recorded. Five are named here because one record named them.

groups.title: The state
groups.note: It licensed the subjects, stamped the blocks, capped the price and moved the theatres.

groups.title: Writers, actors and witnesses
groups.note: The people inside the pictures and the people who wrote down what the trade did.

groups.title: Dealers and collectors
groups.note: The second trade: the people who bought, shipped, sold, copied and gave away.

tsutaya.name: Tsutaya Jūzaburō
tsutaya.cap: Santō Kyōden, caricature of Tsutaya, 1791 · National Diet Library via Wikimedia Commons · public domain (PD-Japan)
tsutaya.line: Born in the Yoshiwara. Publisher of Utamaro, Kyōden and every Sharaku. Fined half of everything he owned in 1791.

nishimuraya.name: Nishimuraya Yohachi (Eijudō)
nishimuraya.line: The Eijudō firm at Bakuro-chō. Published Hokusai’s Thirty-six Views in the new blue, 1831.

iseya.name: Iseya Sōbei
iseya.line: Fan-maker. Put out Keisai Eisen’s all-blue fan in 1829 and started the fad, by Tōho’s account.

hoeido.name: Takenouchi Magohachi (Hōeidō)
hoeido.line: Published Hiroshige’s Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō, 1833–34.

uoya.name: Uoya Eikichi
uoya.line: Published Hiroshige’s One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, 1856–58. His seal reads Shitaya, Uoei.

eirakuya.name: Eirakuya Tōshirō
eirakuya.line: A Nagoya house. Published the Hokusai Manga from 1814.

shioya.name: Shioya Chōbei
shioya.line: Osaka. Granted the sole right to publish actor likenesses in the 8th month of 1793.

moronobu.name: Hishikawa Moronobu
moronobu.line: Signed his book pictures from 1672. The earliest known single-sheet prints follow.

harunobu.name: Suzuki Harunobu
harunobu.line: The designer the poetry circles chose for the full-colour calendars of 1765. No likeness of him survives.

shunsho.name: Katsukawa Shunshō
shunsho.line: Actors with recognisable faces. Hokusai’s first teacher.

utamaro.name: Kitagawa Utamaro
utamaro.cap: Portrait attributed to Chōbunsai Eishi, 1815 · British Museum via Wikimedia Commons · public domain
utamaro.line: Bust portraits of women for Tsutaya in the 1790s. Manacled for fifty days in 1804; dead in 1806.

sharaku.name: Tōshūsai Sharaku
sharaku.line: About 140 actor prints in ten months of 1794–95, all published by Tsutaya. Identity unknown.

ryukosai.name: Ryūkōsai Jokei
ryukosai.line: Osaka. Never signed the prints Shioya published from his designs, and withdrew.

hokusai.name: Katsushika Hokusai
hokusai.cap: Keisai Eisen, portrait of Hokusai · Wikimedia Commons · public domain (PD-Japan)
hokusai.line: Trained to cut woodblocks between 16 and 19. The Manga from 1814; the Fuji series from 1831.

oi.name: Katsushika Ōi
oi.line: Hokusai’s daughter. About ten works confirmed as hers. Her hand is inside work signed “Hokusai” (probable).

eisen.name: Keisai Eisen
eisen.line: His all-blue fan of 1829 started the fad. Van Gogh copied one of his courtesans.

hiroshige.name: Utagawa Hiroshige
hiroshige.cap: Utagawa Kunisada, memorial portrait of Hiroshige, 1858 · The Met, CC0
hiroshige.line: The Tōkaidō of 1833–34. The Hundred Famous Views of Edo, 1856–58.

kuniyoshi.name: Utagawa Kuniyoshi
kuniyoshi.cap: Utagawa Yoshiiku, memorial portrait of Kuniyoshi, 1861 · British Museum via Wikimedia Commons · public domain
kuniyoshi.line: Warriors from 1827, cats always. 408,000 sheets of loyal retainers in eight months.

kunisada.name: Utagawa Kunisada (Toyokuni III)
kunisada.cap: Toyohara Kunichika, memorial portrait of Kunisada · Brooklyn Museum via Wikimedia Commons · public domain
kunisada.line: The most productive designer of actors and beauties of the century.

egawa.name: Egawa Tomekichi
egawa.line: Carver. In 1835 Hokusai gave up his own share of the carving fee to secure him.

kido.name: Kido Kotarō
kido.line: Carver, named in the Smithsonian’s 1889 Tokunō gift.

yamamoto.name: Yamamoto Iwakichi
yamamoto.line: Printer of the Nandina proofs in the Tokunō gift, 1889.

nakamura.name: Nakamura Tsurusaburō
nakamura.line: Printer of the centre sheet of the Tokunō triptych proofs.

morikawa.name: Morikawa Kokichirō
morikawa.line: Recorded as maker of the right sheet of the Tokunō triptych proofs.

ieyasu.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
ieyasu.cap: Portrait attributed to Kanō Tan’yū · Wikimedia Commons · public domain (PD-Japan)
ieyasu.line: Shogun from 1603. Made a marsh-side castle town the seat of government.

sadanobu.name: Matsudaira Sadanobu
sadanobu.line: Chief councillor 1787–93. His reforms put a censor’s seal on every print.

tadakuni.name: Mizuno Tadakuni
tadakuni.cap: Tsubaki Chinzan, portrait of Mizuno Tadakuni · Wikimedia Commons · public domain (PD-Japan)
tadakuni.line: Architect of the Tenpō reforms, 1841–43. Banned actors and courtesans on single sheets.

murata.name: Murata Sahei
murata.line: Ward headman and censor. His seal approved Kuniyoshi’s loyal retainers in 1847.

tokuno.name: Tokunō Michimasa
tokuno.line: Head of the government Printing Bureau. Sent the Smithsonian a complete printing set in 1889.

kyoden.name: Santō Kyōden
kyoden.cap: Eiri, portrait of Santō Kyōden, c. 1795 · The Met, CC0
kyoden.line: Writer as Kyōden, designer as Kitao Masanobu. Fifty days in manacles in 1791.

hanaogi.name: Hanaōgi of the Ōgiya
hanaogi.line: Courtesan, poet and calligrapher. Escaped the quarter in 1794 and was brought back (probable).

danjuro.name: Ichikawa Danjūrō VII
danjuro.cap: Utagawa Kunisada, Danjūrō VII, surimono, 1823 · Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons · public domain
danjuro.line: The theatre’s greatest star. Banished from Edo in 1842 (probable).

toho.name: Seisōdō Tōho
toho.line: Bookseller and memoirist. His Masaki no kazura dates the blue fad to 1829.

fujiokaya.name: Fujiokaya (the diary)
fujiokaya.line: An Edo bookseller’s diary of news. It records the 408,000 sheets of 1847–48, and the flop.

perry.name: Matthew C. Perry
perry.cap: Daguerreotype, Mathew Brady studio · Wikimedia Commons · public domain
perry.line: Commodore. Four ships at Uraga in July 1853; a treaty in 1854.

hayashi.name: Hayashi Tadamasa
hayashi.line: Paris dealer from 1884. 218 shipments of prints and books in eleven years.

bing.name: Siegfried Bing
bing.cap: Photograph before 1906 · Wikimedia Commons · public domain
bing.line: Le Japon artistique, 1888–91. Over 700 prints at the École des Beaux-Arts in 1890.

vangogh.name: Vincent van Gogh
vangogh.cap: Self-Portrait, 1887 · Art Institute of Chicago via Wikimedia Commons · public domain
vangogh.line: Bought about 660 prints in early 1887. Painted three copies that autumn.

fenollosa.name: Ernest Fenollosa
fenollosa.cap: Photograph, c. 1890 · Wikimedia Commons · public domain
fenollosa.line: Boston’s first curator of Japanese art. Curated Japan’s first ukiyo-e exhibition, Tokyo, 1898.

wright.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
wright.cap: Photograph, 1926 · Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons · public domain
wright.line: Architect and print dealer. A Hiroshige show in Chicago, 1906; a scandal, 1920.
